item.title: When an enclave forgets: rollback-resistant registers and the TEE-Rex recovery protocol
item.description: Trusted execution environments (TEEs) such as Intel SGX and ARM TrustZone suggest a shortcut for building fault-tolerant systems. If a replica’s code runs inside a hardware enclave, the replica cannot be made to lie, so a protocol that only tolerates crashes should be enough, and crash tolerance is far cheaper than tolerating arbitrary (Byzantine) behavior. The paper by Sadegh Keshavarzi, Gregory Chockler and Alexey Gotsman, published at DISC 2025, examines a gap in that reasoning. An enclave protects a program while it runs. Once the machine powers off, the state the program saved to disk sits outside that protection, and on restart an attacker can hand the program an older but perfectly authentic copy of it. This is a rollback attack.

item.title: Narwhal and Tusk: Moving the Bottleneck Out of BFT Consensus
item.description: For most of the last decade, work on fast Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) consensus has focused on one number: message complexity, meaning how many protocol messages the validators exchange per decision. HotStuff (Yin et al., 2019) brought that number down to linear in the partially synchronous setting by routing all votes through a leader. The paper by Danezis, Kokoris-Kogias, Sonnino and Spiegelman, published at EuroSys 2022, argues that this target misses where the cost actually sits in a real ledger. The expensive part is not agreeing on an order. It is moving the transactions themselves to every validator, reliably.
